utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is case IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by Mr. Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Defence, please, appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, and Nermin Mulalic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. On Wednesday, 2nd February 2005, the Chamber bids good morning to everybody present in the courtroom; to the Prosecution, to the five Defence lawyers, the accused, as well as the staff of this courtroom, outside and inside of it. We have to continue our work today. I don't have the text, but Mr. Registrar is going to help me. The text on my computer. I don't have the text on the screen. Before we introduce the witness into the courtroom, there is a certain detail that we have to deal with regarding the interpretation. We had a discussion regarding a document in -- that's document P662, and the question was whether the interpretation or the translation of this document was good, and the issue in question was the Mujahedin in the 7th Brigade. In the transcript, in the English and the French transcript -- in the French transcript, I have asked the CLSS to provide us with the translation. In the English transcript this is not reflected. We have issued a memo on the 25th of January -- 27th of January, and we have been provided with an answer. The -- it has been indicated to us that the translation of the B/C/S word into English is "in other words." Do you all have this letter from the CLSS? Mr. Dixon is nodding. The Prosecution should also have it. The Defence of General Hadzihasanovic should also have it. Are there any remarks in this regard? Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood that the translation is not in your favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it's for that reason that I wish to address Your Honours on the matter. We did raise this matter with Your Honours, and if Your Honours recall, at the time Your Honours checked the dictionary meaning of the word and also spoke to the translators at the time about the issue, and you will recall, and it's recorded in the transcript, that Your Honours stated that the word could have a number of meanings. It could mean "in other words," but it could always equally mean "and." So it could read "The 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin." And it very much depends on the context in which the word is used and also the reason why the person who wrote the document used the word as well. Your Honours, we can refer to the transcript where Your Honours made those comments, and we were in full support of the interpretation given to the words by Your Honours. In addition, the witness was then asked, following that remark by Your Honours, about what he meant when he wrote the document. We were very fortunate in that case to have the author of the document, Mr. Sipic, here in court, and he stated that what was meant was the 7th Brigade and the Mujahedin. He said he never meant "in other words." So in our submission, the matter has both been clarified by Your Honours investigating and looking into the matter and by the witness concerned. In our submission, that brings the matter to an end, save to say that we find it somewhat surprising that the CLSS have interpreted this word in this context to mean "in other words," but further down, as I pointed out to Your Honours, where it has the "HVO and their commands," they haven't interpreted that to mean "the HVO in other words their commands." They have used the other meaning of the word, which is "and." In our submission it is the same a few lines above and it should be read like that, especially in light of the evidence we heard on this matter. So in our view the matter has been sufficiently clarified and should not be taken any further given the comments that Your Honours made and the comments that the witness made. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would still like to remind you that when a problem arises, I look at the transcript. We had a break, and after that we resumed at 12 minutes past four, and during the break we looked at the dictionary, B/C/S into Dutch and B/C/S into English, the Benson dictionary that was printed in the United States, and according to Benson, the -- this word could be translated as "in other words." This dictionary also said "more exactly" for the same word. The two dictionary -- during the break, the interpretation service also told us that we could also interpret it as "and." I said on line 21 that at that stage, it was not possible to decide. We asked the Registrar to ask the CLSS to provide us with their view. In the reply that we received, it doesn't state that this word could be translated as "and" but "in other words," which is by no means the same thing. This is where we stand. Mr. Dixon, do you understand? And I know that you are very quick on the uptake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If this document is to be regarded as a final resolution of the matter, then we would seek to take it further. My understanding of the discussion that we'd had earlier on was that Your Honours had, in looking into the matter, noted that it could be read either way and that it depended very much on also what the witness said. But if Your Honours are to regard this, having referred it to the CLSS, as a final word on the matter, a final decision and would seek to admit the document as an exhibit potentially of the Chamber, then we would ask for the matter to be further clarified as we have done with another translation matter, and we would ask them to indicate, that's the CLSS, whether there is an alternative meaning, whether it could also be read as "and the Mujahedin" in much the same way as the words further down are read as "and," "The HVO and the command," and to explain why there is a difference between, if there is one. We say there isn't, but if there is one, why there is a difference between the way the word is used a few lines up and then a few lines down. So we would ask for a further clarification, whether there is another meaning and what that meaning could be. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has heard and understood that the issue has been raised and that the -- if this exhibit is admitted, it will be with the explanation from the CLSS. The Defence now wants us to have another view on the interpretation of this word. Mr. Mundis, what is your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's the Prosecution position that that in fact was what CLSS was asked to do and in fact what CLSS has done as reflected on the memo dated the 27th of January, 2005. They were, in fact, asked to look at this issue. They have done so. I don't intend on engaging in a long discussion as to linguistics, particularly in a language that I don't know, but I will note, Mr. President, that as I'm sure Your Honours are aware, words can be interpreted differently depending upon the context. So it might not be surprising that CLSS would interpret the same word in two different ways depending upon the context in which the word appears on the document. If the Chamber deems it necessary to send the document back to CLSS and ask them to look at it again, that certainly is within the Trial Chamber's purview, but our position is, as it was previously, that the CLSS has been asked to do this, they have done so. We would object, as we indicated when this issue arose, that we don't believe that CLSS should be particularly notified or pointed to the testimony of the witness and some 12 years later explaining what he meant in the document. We believe that the document, in effect, speaks for itself. The Defence have raised an issue as to some ambiguity in the document. CLSS was asked to take another look at it, and they have come to a conclusion. Furthermore, we would object if the Defence either now or in the future seeks to have some outside translation service look at the document. I will simply note at this point in time that we would object to that and if that's the course the Defence seeks to go down, we would like to be heard further on that particular issue. But our view is, Mr. President, this has been requested, and it's been done, and the result is before you, and we believe that that settles the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I'm turning towards the Defence. I -- we have discussed this among the Judges, and we think that we should take into consideration this quote, this disputed quote, and I believe that we could obtain further information about the word "odnosno." We will forward all that to the CLSS who will, after having been informed of the position of the Defence and after having looked at the document itself, will provide us with another opinion. The Prosecution has just told us that he would object to any outside interpretation. We can appreciate that, because in this institution there is a service. The translators are professionals, experts in a number of languages. Mr. Dixon, I'm going to give you the floor as the last speaker on this subject, and after that the Judges will deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would request -- it appears that Your Honours are indicating that this will be sent further to CLSS for a further inquiry, that the discussions that we've had today are forwarded to the CLSS as well, because all this document says is that this is a revised translation. There's no explanation given, and we would request that there is some explanation given as to why that word can have such different meanings, if at all, and certainly to look at whether there can be an alternative meaning and to what extent the context of the whole sentence comes into play. So a further explanation is required. And if they could also look at how that compares to the way the word is used a few lines down. I think that would be helpful for -- for the Court in considering this matter. Leaving aside what the witness has said, I agree with my learned friend that we have to resolve the translation separately at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The three Judges will discuss the issue, and we will inform you about our decision on this matter. We're going to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue in open session. We have to deal with the issue of exhibits, of Defence exhibits and maybe Prosecution exhibits as well. Defence, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. After the testimony of Colonel Stewart that finished yesterday during which we used a series of documents, the Defence would like the following documents to be admitted. I have a list before me. This list was at the beginning of the binder. A number of these documents have already been admitted. The Defence wants the following to be admitted into evidence: Document number 5 under tab 5. This is document 1721 for which we seek admission into evidence. The next one is document under tab 6, DH630 ID. Then under tab 7, DH648, which has already been given a mark for identification. Document under tab 8. This is a new document which was used with the permission of the Chamber. The date of the document is 25 January 1993, and the title of the document is Situation in Gornji Vakuf, in English. Document under tab 9 is DH612. This document has already been marked for identification. Document under tab 10, 1732. Document under tab 11, number DH632 ID, again a document marked for identification already. Document under tab 12, DH633 ID, for identification. Document under tab 13, DH634 ID -- ID, another document that has been marked for identification. Document under tab 14 is a new document which was used with the Chamber's permission. The date of the document is 26 January 1993, and its title is Milinfosum Number 87. Document under tab 15, number 1 -- DH1738 ID for identification. The following document is under tab 22. This document bears the number DH726 ID. The document under tab 23, DH740 ID, for identification. Document under 26. The number is 1783. And finally, the document under tab 27, a new document used with the Chamber's permission. The date on this document is 24 April 1993, and its title is HVO Information. The Defence would like all these documents to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These are being admitted as exhibits under the following numbers: The first document, DH1721. It doesn't have a B/C/S version. The original is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You made a mistake. You said 1720, but it is 1721.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document DH630 is admitted into evidence, with its English version, 630/E. DH648 is admitted into evidence under the Exhibit number DH648/E. A new document, dated the 25th of January, 1993, entitled UNPROFOR Situation in Gornji Vakuf, is admitted as DH2009, the document being in English. DH612 is admitted into evidence, and its English translation, 612/E. DH1732 is admitted into evidence, and the English version, 1732/E. DH632 is admitted into evidence, and its English version DH632/E. Document DH633 is admitted into evidence, and its English version bearing the number 633/E. Document DH634 is admitted into evidence, and its English version bearing the number 634/E. The document dated the 26th of January, 1993, entitled Milinfosum 87 is admitted as DH2010, the original being in English. Document DH1738 is admitted into evidence, and its English version 1738/E. DH726 is admitted into evidence, and its English version bearing the exhibit number 726/E. DH740 admitted into evidence, and its English version DH740/E. Document DH1783 is admitted into evidence, and the English version 1783/E. And finally, at the end of this list, the document dated the 24th of April, 1993, entitled HVO Information is admitted into as an exhibit, DH2011, and the English version being DH2011/E. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. You have given us the exhibit numbers for these documents now. I turn to the Prosecution now to see whether they have any documents to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have three documents that we would simply request at this point in time be marked for identification and not admitted into evidence. The first of these was the Milinfosum dated 27 January 1993. The second document was the Milinfosum dated 11 March 1993. And the third document is the HVO document dated 18 April 1993 that was signed by Colonel Blaskic. All three of these documents the witness -- these documents were all put to the witness yesterday, and at this point in time, Mr. President, we would simply ask that they be marked for identification and attached to the record of these proceedings. And before I give the floor to the Defence, Mr. President, we do have two other issues relating to this witness that we would like to raise perhaps after the documents but before the next witness comes into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution is asking to tender three documents to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No objection on the part of the Defence for these documents to be marked identification. If these documents may be tendered into evidence finally, then the Defence reserves the right to make certain statements, submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours will be aware of my submissions yesterday. In our submission, none of these documents can be used to strengthen the case of the Prosecution. They were used as memory-refreshing documents. But as the witness was not able to comment on them as documents that did refresh his memory, in our view they are not documents that should become part of the evidence in this case and therefore we would oppose them being marked for identification even at this stage. They have been referred to on the record and the witness has commented on them and there is no need for the documents to be entered into evidence in any form whatsoever, including identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will subsequently deliberate on the fate of these documents. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would simply like to make a point of clarification, as the Defence of Hadzihasanovic takes the same position as the Defence of the accused Kubura only we expressed ourselves differently. In our opinion, when a document is marked for identification, that document cannot be used with another witness because it is in the file, but it would always be a new document. It does not lose its status of a new document. Therefore, in our view, marked for identification really doesn't mean anything. However, as a document has been admitted and marked for identification, it cannot be used with another witness. It always remains a new document if it is to be used with a subsequent witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Prosecution wishes to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Our view is -- is a very different one in an important aspect. Our view clearly, Mr. President, is that a document that's marked for identification is not evidence and is not something that the Trial Chamber could rely upon until and unless the document is tendered and admitted by Your Honours into evidence. The sole purpose of marking the document and appending it to the record is so that later, either during the remaining course of the trial or perhaps in any appeal, if recourse needs to be had to the document to compare it, for example, with what the witness testified about, the document is readily available for everyone because it's part of the proceedings. Let me just address one final issue. And for that very reason, to address the point raised by my learned friend Mr. Bourgon, if we wanted to show the same document to a subsequent witness, the fact that it has a number makes that much simpler to follow in the subsequent proceedings by way of the transcript. It doesn't mean by showing it to one, five, or ten witnesses down the road that the document becomes part of the evidence. Is simply means it's a shorthand way of referring to a document so that throughout the remainder of the proceedings everyone knows that the document with this date from this person to that person has a number. We very well might seek to show some of the documents that have been marked for identification to subsequent witnesses, but it doesn't -- the document doesn't become evidence, in our view, until we tender it and Your Honours admit it into evidence. It's simply a shorthand way of marking a document so that everyone knows what document we're talking about when we refer to it by a number. That's all that it means, in our view, to mark a document for identification. It's marking it for identification. It doesn't become evidence. And our view would be, as the Defence have done with documents that have been previously marked for identification, you show them to witnesses. If the witness has nothing to add, perhaps the document doesn't go into evidence. But it's simply a shorthand way of marking the document. It's not evidence until it's tendered and admitted, and I think that I everyone agrees on that. It's simply a shorthand way of marking a document and our view is we should be able to show these documents to subsequent witnesses and perhaps even in reopening our case or in rebuttal we'll seek to tender them, perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution explained why they would like documents to be marked for identification. The Prosecution tells us that there are two fundamental reasons, the first being that during a cross-examination to test credibility, the Prosecution may show a document to a witness to hear his comments. In the future, should the Appeals Chamber perhaps be approached - I am talking about a hypothesis for the future - for the Judges to be able to appreciate the content of the transcript and what the witness said, they need to compare it with the document. So there is this final requirement, judicial requirement, hence the position of the Prosecution that the document be marked for identification and be part of the record to allow the Judges to check the substance of the witness's statement. That is the first consideration. And the second is that if there is a number, when future witnesses come it will be easier for the Prosecution to say, "I'm going to show to Witness X a document, PY ID," and then instead of the registrar spending minutes looking for it, he will be able to find it easily. So those are the two considerations. And as this is something quite new, I would like the Defence to convey their opinion to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think there is no dispute when we're talking about the use of a document filed in this way. That is why we have no objection for a document to be marked for identification, and that remains our position. However, when those documents were shown to the witness, they were discussed, that is, why a new document which does not appear in the file could be shown to a particular witness. In the hypothesis that a new witness appears and we want to use that document once again, the same discussion will arise, that is the conditions imposed by the Chamber regarding the use of new documents arise again, that is, permission is required to be able to use that document with that new witness. As for the use of the Appeals Chamber of these documents, I don't think we need to go into that at this stage, and I would not like to present any arguments of substance regarding the use of documents by the Appeals Chamber. I would prefer to reserve my right to make my submissions on that point at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, you will certainly provide clarifications for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There's no problem from our side giving the document a number so that it can be retrieved or used in the future, but in our submission it should be given a number for identification but marked as a new document to distinguish it from the other documents. In other words, this is a document which was not introduced during the Prosecution case. It's a new document. So that when it is retrieved, that is the status of the document. And as my learned friend has said, Mr. Bourgon, at any time when it is to be used for a new witness proper grounds have to be established, either credibility or memory refreshing, and that is an entirely separate issue, as Your Honours have indicated, as to whether it is to be admitted or not. And even if it is to be admitted at some point, in our submission it can only be admitted for the purposes of credibility or memory refreshing as has been done in the past. Of course it's a different question if my learned friend seeks to open his case or bring it in rebuttal, but our main point is that it cannot be introduced at this stage to strengthen the case of the Prosecution or to go to the individual criminal responsibility of the accused in this case. That is the thrust of Your Honours' ruling, and we wish that to be respected. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have heard the opinions of all parties, and the Judges will decide as to what should be done as you have had occasion to express your views at length on these points. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecution, but we will go back into private session once again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your testimony will start shortly. Before that, I have to provide you with some information as to how your testimony will develop. First of all, you're going to be given a piece of paper on which you will put your first name, your last name, and XC and today's date -- I'm sorry, HC and today's date. Can you do it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to put my first name and last name plus HC?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And today's date. Today we are the 2nd February, 2005. The 2nd February. We will show this piece of paper to the Prosecution, to the Defence teams, to the accused. This document will be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number will be admitted as DH21 -- 2013 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be asked to answer questions put to you by the Defence within the frame of their examination-in-chief. This will last about an hour. After that stage, which will last for an hour, the Prosecution, on your right, will also put questions to you within the frame of what we call cross-examination. This is something that you should be familiar with because it's part of the common law procedure. The Prosecution will also be given an hour. After that, the Defence lawyer will be given an opportunity to ask you additional questions during re-examination. The questions that will be put to you during that stage will be directly connected with the questions put to you by the Prosecution during their cross-examination in chief. In order to avoid problems that we encountered yesterday, questions put in redirect should not be leading questions. This is how your testimony should develop. After these stages, the Judges that are in front of you, according to the rules and procedures of this Tribunal, can ask you any questions they might think are useful for establishing the truth. The Judges are independent, and they ask their questions in order to establish the truth. After the questions put to you by the Judges, the two parties can show you documents in order to refresh your memory and to obtain your views on these documents to the extent that you may be familiar with them. I would also like to inform you two other elements. First of all, you have taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, which means you are not to give us false testimony because this is punishable by the law. This is what I tell all the witnesses. And there is another thing that I tell all the witnesses, although this may not apply to you. A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate him or her. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question and the testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony. This is something that is common practice in the United States but also in your country. We are in the so-called accusatory proceedings, which are oral proceedings complemented by the documents provided during the hearings. We do not have any prior documents, so your words are very important. Before you answer any questions, take your time to think about the question and answer only if you believe that you have understood the question. If a question seems to be too complicated, you can always ask the person who has put it to you to rephrase it. If you have any difficulties, do not hesitate to signal to the Chamber that you are experiencing those difficulties. And finally, for the reasons of interpretation and the logistics of this courtroom, we are obliged to make a break every hour and a half. Since we started at 9.00, we will have to make our first break in 15 minutes, and after a 25-minute break, we shall resume and we shall go on for the next hour and a half. To -- we are certain that we will be able to finish your testimony today, which will enable you to go back home today. This is more or less what I am supposed to tell you before your testimony begins. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence lawyer who is going to be putting questions to you. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness HC. Although we have had the opportunity of meeting before your testimony today, for the benefit of the transcript, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and this morning I am accompanied with my colleague Mrs. Edina Residovic from Sarajevo and Mr. Alexis Demirdjian from Montreal, and together we represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic. I have some questions to put to you today with respect, as we have discussed previously, your deployment to Bosnia in 1992/1993. Before I do that, I would like to ask you a few questions which I will basically lead through your career, and if you can just acknowledge whether these issues or these facts that I'm about to mention correspond to your career.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to go into private session just to check the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, you mentioned a little earlier that you had deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992. Can you first provide us, which dates exactly did you deploy to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Deployed actually on the 7th November 1992 to Bosnia via Split and then returning on the 6th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who did you work for during this mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I deployed as the direct liaison officer interpreter to the command of British forces for the former Yugoslavia, Brigadier Andrew Cumming, initially in Divulje barracks in Split before them moving later on into Central Bosnia to work alongside the Cheshire battle group, and then in Eastern Bosnia along with General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the commander of British forces. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what -- who exactly is the commander of British forces and whether there is a link between the commander of the British forces, or what is the link between the commander of British forces and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As part of the UN mandate, Britain was requested to provide a British Battalion. That was to be in the form of the 1st Battalion of the 22nd Cheshire Regiment, however all national contingents deployed supporting elements in the form of a formation level headquarters, in this case a brigade that will deploy from Germany to essentially provide the national link between the United Nations and our permanent joint headquarters based in English itself. And so essentially the British Battalion deployed as part of the UN mandate although the British element was not formally part of the UN mandate, it was there in a supporting role. So essentially the chain of command was from BritBat directed back to the United Kingdom where the British Battalion, in the case of the Cheshires, had two chains of command; one to UNPROFOR and one then back to BRITFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, can you further explain whether this is a procedure that was followed by other states or was this a procedure that was unique to the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was followed by other states. Certainly Divulje barracks was a compound in Split which had a number of national contingents based there from which they were commanded. Some contingents only had minor staff who actually integrate as part of the UN headquarters, be they in Sarajevo or elsewhere, but essentially we had a brigade sized formation headquarters in Split to coordinate British activities at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what were your duties working with the commander of British forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially we obviously deployed -- the brigade deployed itself towards the end of October. I was deployed to be the interpreter and main liaison officer for the brigadier himself, essentially speaking -- having knowledge of the language, the culture and the geography, I was his asset in terms of facilitating meetings, acting as an interpreter when required, and basically doing activities to facilitate operational deployments and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, was there a reason why you were selected for this deployment working with the commander of British forces in Bosnia despite the fact that you were relatively, I guess, a junior officer at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Britain was informed that we would send troops to the former Yugoslavia, we had a shortage of fluent linguists to support the operation itself, so as has been previously mentioned, I was already in Northern Ireland on operational deployment and essentially it was found out I could speak the language because of my cultural upbringing, knowing the people, the geography, essentially speaking, was seen to be a valuable assess to the army, and so I was one of three people deployed to Bosnia at that time to act as interpreter and liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I ask you in terms of upon deploying with the British forces at that time, how much did the British forces really know before deploying about the situation they were getting into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In reality very little. It was a very confused situation. We had very little warning of actually when we were going to be deploying and where we were to go. I certainly recall in October being notified the original plan was to move through Serbia via Loznica and establish ourselves in the Tuzla area, and basically the plan changed on a regular basis. Really it was at the last minute that we actually found out what we were doing, but across the army as whole there was very little knowledge about what was going on in Yugoslavia and it was for that reason we were called in to assist commanders to provide the background knowledge, the advice, and really the expertise based on our experience, albeit relatively junior officers, in terms of actually what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now you yourself, Witness HC, did the commander of British forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina was looking to benefit from your linguistic ability or from your cultural knowledge of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was both, really. I mean, at the end of the day we were totally reliant, in most cases, to locally employed interpreters and translators, and therefore having an officer who could speak the language and then essentially you could deal on a one-to-one basis purely military aspects and therefore you were trusted, as opposed to trusting solely an interpreter whose integrity could not always be relied upon necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how important was this to the commander of British forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was fundamental not only from a perspective of the presentational aspects to be able to go into a military headquarters with one of your own officers who could speak the language and therefore in a closed session be bound by the terms of what was agreed at the meeting, it was a great advantage. Also, at the end of the day, you know, I could be deployed, or one of the other two individuals could be deployed as individuals to act independently to basically ensure that the day-to-day in the command was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during your tour in Bosnia and Herzegovina and during that period, did you always work with commander of British forces or were you also -- did you also have the opportunity to work with other organisations in theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With other organisations. Basically, we were in quite short supply and therefore were sent around the whole of the country where we were actually required. As said, initially we deployed, worked exclusively for the command of British forces, we then deployed with the engineer element to establish the routes from Croatia into Bosnia from Tomislavgrad back to Prozor, I was involved in negotiations there. As soon as the Cheshire battle group deployed into Central Bosnia the need was felt that I should be with them to basically act as a liaison officer interpreter, and then in the beginning of 1993 when the situation around Eastern Bosnia, particularly Srebrenica, was becoming tense I was then deployed into that region to establish the mission there to facilitate the aid convoys from Belgrade to Tuzla, and then I was attached to General Morillon in his exploits in the Srebrenica area around March 1993, before then returning again back into Central Bosnia, again used by the chief of staff of UNPROFOR, Brigadier Roddy Cordy-Simpson, as his interpreter on occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness HC.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm looking at the time. I believe the -- it is now the time for our technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We should resume around five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I give the floor to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Witness HC. Just before I ask you my next question, I would just like to remind you, at the break I was warned that we are both speaking way too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So let us both try to make an effort for the sake of the interpreters and the people taking the transcript. Before the break, Witness HC, you mentioned that you had been, during your tour in Bosnia, working with -- at times with BritBat, at times with General Morillon, and of course with your main employer commander of British forces. My question, then, is when working for these people, did you have the opportunity to attend any meetings with the representatives of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever a meeting was held, I would either go, depending on the situation, as an interpreter to the meeting -- for example, if it was between two sides who didn't get on, and at the time we were employing predominantly Bosnian Muslim locals as our interpreters, so on some occasions, particularly with the Serbs, no one could go therefore I would go to these meetings. When the problems then started to build up between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims again we couldn't take certain interpreters onto the ground. That was my responsibility. But essentially if I was in a particular area at any one time, the commander would normally ask for my presence at these meetings, not necessarily to interpret but to sit there to listen to what was being said on the sidelines and provide advice and assistance to, you know, the individual officers in the course of their duties. So if I was in the area I would tend to be invited to these meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Looking at the HVO in 1993, did you have -- did you attend any meetings with high-level representatives of the HVO; and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of our meetings at that time were conducted around the Lasva Valley area, so on the regular basis we would meet with Colonel Tihomir Blaskic who was in the operational command of the elements in Central Bosnia there. On a political level we would tend to meet with Dario Kordic, who was obviously operating in that area also, particularly around the Busovaca area. Only really at later stages in our tour did we actually then engage in conversations and negotiations with the likes of General Petkovic, who was brought into the region to be sure that the various agreements were adhered to by local commanders. So on a day-to-day basis the British themselves and myself would deal with the likes of Kordic and/or Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Mr. Kordic, can you, without going into too many details, provide the Trial Chamber with your assessment of his contribution to the situation in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His contribution, whenever we met with the HVO, it was very much a political and a military meeting in many respects. So if ever we met with Kordic, Blaskic would be there or one of Blaskic's subordinates, and vice versa. Kordic himself was a political figure, certainly when speaking to local Bosnian Muslims. They blamed him for many of the problems that were associated with that region and certainly stoking up the flames in many respects in terms of causing the various problems. Very outspoken at all times, wasn't a particularly likable man. To a certain extent he was very right wing, racist towards the Bosnian Muslims, and when meeting him he was very difficult to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at Blaskic, in the meetings when you had the opportunity to see him, can you describe him without going into too many details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly in those early days he was by rank a colonel although in terms of his rank he attained that rank quite quickly once the war started. He was a relatively junior officer in what was the Yugoslav People's Army. And he lacked, towards personally, that operational knowledge in terms of the wider context of command and control in warfare. He's probably a very good tactical commander but heavily influenced by the political aspect to the HVO who really, in our view, held the real purse strings in terms of what people could or could not do, and certainly towards the latter stages of April, he was a very nervous individual because the events that transpired in Central Bosnia at times were backfiring against the Croats and therefore they feared for their future in many respects because they realised their actions were causing more problems than they were worth. So you know, he was perfectly amicable to deal with but obviously he had higher echelons who actually dictated what was going on to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you attended any meetings, who were they with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a daily basis, we would really deal with local commanders, normally at brigade level, on the grounds that they were physically in command of the elements on the ground themselves. Quite regularly we would have meetings with 3 Corps, with the general or the general's subordinates, an individual by the name of Merdan, but on a daily basis it tended to be at the lower levels because they're the ones who were actually holding the ground who we obviously need to speak to on a daily basis to find out what was going on in their areas in the same way as the local Croatian commanders, but predominantly with local Bosniak commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned the general. Which general are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to meet on a regular basis, or how many times did you have the opportunity to meet with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause, please, between question and answer. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many times would you have met with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met on a regular basis. The problem I had was I was flitting at that time between operations in Central Bosnia and Eastern Bosnia, so if I was in the right place at the right time and Colonel Bob Stewart would go to a meeting in Zenica or the general visits Vitez or other areas, if I was there I would go to those meetings, so met on a very regular basis but sufficient to get the know the general reasonably well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how would you assess or describe General Hadzihasanovic in his capacity as commander of the 3rd Corps in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously not knowing the general before the conflict, first impressions count. He actually made the effort to come visit us in Vitez on -- soon after the arrival of the battle group in the area, and you know, first impression was that he was a classic officer of the mould of the Yugoslav army at the time; very decent, professional individual, very respectful, and straight away offered his full cooperation in terms of our mission there, which was for us a great advantage. I think more importantly he said his office was always open to the planning office of the battle group and he never refused our sort of approaches to him to find out what was going on, and if he was in Zenica when we were there, we'd either call in or certainly the colonel would call in and he'd always be there or provide an officer to meet us. So very cooperative and a very decent man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the name Merdan. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, who is Merdan and what is your assessment of Merdan in terms of when you had meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you'll appreciate on a day-to-day basis it wasn't always possible to drag the general away from his duties and so our main point of contact at the battalion level was Merdan himself. He was obviously a key subordinate to the general himself, and certainly when we started doing more and more work in terms of joint work with the commission to do with the Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, he was the point of contact who would be responsible for ensuring that what was ordered from the corps was carried out on the ground itself, and he was always at the disposal of ourselves, you know, if we required him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And based on your experience in 1993, was Merdan respected in and out of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean I don't ever recall, certainly from the HVO side, any complaints being made about Merdan himself or General Hadzihasanovic. It was always one of respect in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, quickly, can you tell us, because you mentioned the name a little earlier, I believe you said Cordy-Simpson. Can you tell us who he is and what his function was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UNPROFOR itself at that time was commanded by General Philippe Morillon, who was a French officer. Morillon's style was very much to be on the ground, literally everywhere, meeting with politicians, commanders. This was an absolute nightmare for the headquarters in Kiseljak on the grounds that the general who commanded the operation was rarely in his headquarters, so the role of the chief of staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina command was fundamental to the day-to-day running of the United Nations mission in Bosnia. For whatever reason, the chief of staff was always a British officer and during the time that we were there, it was Brigadier Roddy Cordy-Simpson and he was a crucial player in terms of actually facilitating physical operations on ground while the general was really going around making sure all the various parties involved in the conflict were doing what they should be doing, so on a day-to-day basis, Brigadier Roddy Cordy-Simpson was fundamental to the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again, Witness HC, I'm going to ask you to try and slow down a bit when you speak. And my next question is whether you had any dealings with lieutenant colonel or then Lieutenant Colonel Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commanding officer of the British Battalion based in Vitez, and as I've already said, initially deployed specifically to support Brigadier Cumming in Split, but as soon as the mission was established in Central Bosnia on a day-to-day basis I was working under the operational control of the British Battalion but command of the BRITFOR element. So if I was in Vitez, I would always be with the colonel at various meetings or deployments onto the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of assessing from your point of view and experience Lieutenant Colonel Stewart as commander of the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart was a very senior lieutenant colonel. In fact he'd been promoted to the rank of full colonel, I believe, immediately prior to the deployment, but requested to remain as a commanding officer as a lieutenant colonel for the duration. Very professional officer, very charismatic. The right officer for the job at that time in terms of ensuring that the job was done but also, more importantly, in terms of the public perception of what we were doing back in England, and so he became very much a personality. He was always on the news. Became very, dare I say, emotionally involved in terms of the plight of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was not shy in going forward, would berate people publicly, would tell them exactly what he thought, and made a lot of enemies, I believe, in Bosnia, particularly with some local commanders, and there was a great deal of jealousy back in England, certainly amongst our seniors officers who at times were very critical of him but because of his public standing could do very little against him. I know of two occasions where basically he was brought for interviews without coffee, as we say, for his actions but on every occasion he was able to demonstrate exactly why he carried those actions and what benefit it made on the ground. So the right man for the job at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness HC, can you tell from the times you were with Colonel Stewart whether he was the kind of man who would hesitate to bring forward any complaints to any of the warring factions in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean, he was very, you know, emotional. He was obviously a human being and if he thought something was wrong or a crime had been committed, he literally told as it was and therefore would have no hesitation in exposing the facts to individuals concerned and trying to, you know, achieve justice in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness HC, Colonel Stewart actually testified before this Trial Chamber yesterday, and he mentioned an incident arising close to Kacuni in Central Bosnia on the 25th of January having to do with a roadblock established by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you recall whether you were with Bob Stewart on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was. One of the criticisms levelled against the colonel was the fact that he on many occasions personally led operations on the ground where normally as a commanding officer he would sit back to allow subordinates to get on with the job, but his style was to be there on the ground himself and so because at that time the whole Lasva Valley was a tense area, pockets of Croats and Muslims basically from one end to the other, in Kacuni itself it was a tense situation because of the situation resulting in the Bosnian Muslims being surrounded by Bosnian Croats. The actual route from Busovaca to Kiseljak was blocked by a roadblock established on the bridge in Kacuni. The roadblock itself was a lorry full of logs, and we'd already received from 3rd Corps assurances from General Hadzihasanovic that the roadblock would be lifted. However, the soldiers on the ground testified to us that the roadblock was still in place. We repeatedly went back to 3 Corps to demand that the roadblock be lifted and were given assurances that order had been given to the local commander that the roadblock would be lifted, and again it never happened. We then personally went to the ground and it was clearly the commander on the ground who was refusing to obey the order given to him by General Hadzihasanovic on the grounds that he felt threatened by the situation physically on the ground there and by removing the roadblock he would expose essentially the entry into the Kacuni area to the HVO. So despite assurances given us to by 3 Corps we eventually managed -- I can't remember exactly when happened, but to convince the Bosnians to move the roadblock to allow our vehicles through and they then closed the road again with the same obstacle, and it was at that time that we were essentially berating the local commander, telling him that he should be listening to the orders from 3 Corps, that one of his soldiers had a negligent discharge, he fired into the ground accidentally with his rifle, we thought we were under fire from the HVO positions, we clearly weren't, and interestingly, my toe of my boot was shot off in the process, so a memorable incident in that respect, but illustrated the problem we had on the ground at that time in terms of the passage of information from a corps level to a brigade level down to, you know, physical soldiers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Witness HC, would you recall what you did on that occasion or following this event after going through that roadblock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We remained, if I recall, on the ground for a while, and shortly afterwards we were visited by Brigadier Roddy Cordy-Simpson, and I can't remember the exact circumstances but for whatever reason then I found myself in Kiseljak with the brigadier working for him for a short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the days that followed, do you remember attending any specific meeting where the parties were discussing any specific issue of importance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, because of the fighting between the Croats and the Muslims, all the various discussions were about acts that had been committed by one side or the other or essentially, you know, the breaking down of any agreements that were in place. And so I attended a meeting chaired by the brigadier in the presence of Colonel Blaskic as well as other officers and political figures. I wasn't an interpreter. I was sat by his side and to basically let him know what was being said in the sidelines because, as the interpreters will verify, they can't essentially interpret everything that is said in the meeting, it's only the official aspects of it, so my role was to basically feed the brigadier with additional information that was being said, either in the written form or verbally, about that was -- you know, what was being said on the sidelines. And during the course of that meeting, when things were going particularly well for the Bosnian Croat delegation, I recall distinctly someone entered the room with a written note, gave it to one of Blaskic's subordinates, I can't exactly remember the words that were said apart from to the extent that tell them that Busovaca has been attacked, it's on fire, and we should end the meeting. At that point I quickly informed the brigadier what had been said before the interpreter could actually say anything, and it was then that the brigadier, who quite often would lose his temper, lost his temper on that occasion and basically told the Croats to remain seated while he verified exactly what was going on in Busovaca at that time. He obviously sent word to one of our call-signs, our units in the Busovaca area, who shortly afterwards returned to say that actually the accusation of attacking Busovaca and that Busovaca was in flames actually wasn't true, and therefore the meeting continued. And if I recall, as a result of that meeting the agreement was established for the establishment of a joint commission to go from one area to another to basically work out what was going on and to basically stop the fuel on the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember why you were at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, I don't recall why I was asked to go there, but clearly having witnessed this event it was clear that the brigadier intended me to inform him what was going on and therefore him not to be ambushed by the other side in that respect in terms of their intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like now to show you a document which deals with this meeting. This is document DH0664, and I have sufficient copies for everyone in the courtroom. There are only four documents or five which I wish to use today and they can be distributed in a bundle to all the parties. They are being given to you in the order in which they will be used. Now, Witness HC I will ask you to look at this document and tell me whether this is the meeting you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, looking at the meeting itself, do you recall what happened at points 4 and 5 of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, we have an illegible text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is the best we could do. The original is also very poor. It is just as bad, in fact. I think, Mr. President, that we're going to ask another version to be produced so that we can read it to read the paragraph that we need, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to read paragraph 4 and 5 and do you recall these events being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 is quite difficult to read. I wasn't present at the meeting referred to on the 26th of January. I was only present at the meeting on the 27th. But I recall both sides at the meeting referring to incidents that had taken place but I had no knowledge of those at the time and the fact that essentially speaking as a result of that meeting it was agreed that the situation as summarised in paragraph 6 was the case and that the joint commission would be established in accordance with paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I bring to you paragraph 8 -- sorry, paragraph 9 of this document, can you tell us if this is the incident that you described a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the incident. And Brigadier Cordy-Simpson's view was that the incident was a deliberate ploy to derail the meeting when it was obviously becoming quite crucial and by really sort of, you know, stopping them before they could act. We basically ensured that the meeting was completed and obviously that the findings were within this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you to paragraph 11 of the same document and can you recall the actions that are described at paragraph 11 of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The key factor at that time was that both sides were alleging that the other side was breaking all the rules of any agreements and were in violation of various cease-fires, and therefore what we required was independent verification on the ground. At the end of the day it got to the stage where we couldn't believe certain sides in terms of what they were saying and so it was agreed that both of the HVO and the 3rd Corps would have members attached to a joint commission run by the ECMM and also a British officer who would essentially go around mapping where the front line was and going to incidents which had occurred to basically pacify the situation. So that was a positive step which we then took further forward, as a result, throughout the whole of Bosnia towards 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness HC, this commission being tasked to report to a further meeting, as described in paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The plan was that as a result of their initial reports their findings would be given to the UN at a subsequent meeting few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now ask you to look at the next document, which is P922, and tell me if you recall this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this meeting. This was a meeting that took place after the meeting in Kiseljak, which is really the first opportunity for the monitoring mission to report. It took place in the British camp in Vitez with quite a lot of sort of fanfare, a lot of media interest, and as a result they reported. Although I personally for that occasion wasn't in the meeting because it wasn't -- I wasn't physically needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you did not attend the meeting, why would you remember the holding of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Purely because, you know, it was the first time that the ECMM had arrived in the camp and there were a lot of journalists there at the time and at home I've got a photograph of it in my photo album.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move on to the next issue, and I was wondering if in your capacity as advisor to commander of British forces you developed any knowledge of the Vance-Owen Plan during your stay in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. As I already mentioned, there was across the army a lack of understanding what was going on in terms of the situation in the whole of Yugoslavia. Right from the beginning, because of my personal background and my family connections, I really made it my business to know what was going on there, and there were so many different initiatives with a view of bringing the war to an end that had failed, and really the Vance-Owen Peace Plan that was put forward by Cyrus Vance and David Owen was really the first step in terms of trying to get an agreement in place. But when you looked at the actual plan in terms of whether it was achievable on the physical ground, those who knew anything about the conflict knew that not all sides would agree to it. The prospect of establishing ten cantons based on ethnicity was going to cause all sorts of problems. From a Serbian perspective, it meant that the east would not be linked to the west because between them in the Brcko area would be a Bosnian Muslim canton and therefore, as far as the Greater Serbian aims were concerned, they would therefore be broken, and so as a result of that, you know, critics will say straight away that the plan was going to fail. However, the principles were accepted but, regrettably, the Serbs then rejected it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness HC, can you recall the attitude of the HVO towards the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as the Vance-Owen Plan was mooted and being discussed one of the first actions we saw on the ground was instead of talking about Bosnia as a state, all of a sudden Herceg-Bosna was being established particularly in the southern areas. It was as if the Croatian cantons were therefore going to be permanent and their requirement was that any Bosnian Muslim forces that well within the cantonal areas were to be then integrated within the HVO and those who refused to integrate would surrender their weapons and leave, and clearly this caused a great deal of tension, particularly in Central Bosnia. The other drama, of course, as a result of that, the increased tension in those areas where the Croats themselves were finding themselves in the Bosnian Muslim cantons, and so it was a recipe for disaster and it was one of the reasons why -- in fact, it was a catalyst for the violence that we suddenly found ourselves in in Central Bosnia around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness HC, what were you told before deploying as to the relationship between the HVO and the ABiH? What did you find out on the ground, and what were the consequences for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly across the world the Serbian side was seen to be the main aggressor, the victims in Bosnia were therefore perceived to be the Croats, the Muslims, who themselves were fighting together to repel the Serbs. Those who know anything about the past will recall that essentially Serbs had by this stage, by September, October, managed to capture about 6 per cent of the territory to consolidate. They were therefore very stretched in terms of their front line and couldn't physically hold the entire front line all the time. We then deployed, still assuming that the Bosnians and the Muslims were obviously friendly towards each other, but shortly after our deployment Prozor, a town very close to Central Bosnia, was ethnically cleansed by the Croats and the Muslim population driven out, which came was a shock to the British forces at that time. That then had repercussions particularly in the area around Bugojno and elsewhere and then we suddenly realised that the underlying tensions were always going to be in that region itself, and so from our perspective that tension was a surprise. As far as the Serbs are concerned, this suited their aims on the ground, so that rather than doing the fighting themselves, they could leave the Croats and Muslims to kill themselves, which suited them. Bizarrely enough, on many occasions, particularly around the Bugojno area and also towards Mostar, the Serbs themselves supported the Croats by either donating military equipment -- and I'll never forget on the road to Sarajevo seeing Serb tanks being handed over to the Croats for 24 hours and seeing them then being returned, and also fire missions are requested quite often by the Croats from the Serbs to support their attacks against the Bosnian Muslims. So it was a very bizarre situation. And for the Muslims themselves, we felt sorry for them because they not only had a front against the Serbs but now also had a front against the Croats and were pretty well landlocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness HC, what was the status of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't particularly good. With great respect to them, they were pretty well unprepared for the war, although from my own personal belief, you know, the war was inevitable based on what their political aims were in terms of breaking away from Yugoslavia. However, very few people felt the war was going to happen whereas the Bosnian Serbs themselves were able -- able to sort of to maintain that the integrity of what was the Yugoslav army within Bosnia, the Croats are supported very much so from Croatia proper, but the Bosnian Muslims themselves were badly equipped. A great deal of manpower but in terms of military capability, particularly in terms of the commanders on the ground, were very limited. It was also a bizarre organisation whereby you had corps commanders basically working directly to brigade commanders and field commanders on the ground. We would normally have, in the Western society, divisional headquarters to basically be linked between the various aspects but in that case it was very much personality based, and the drama the Bosnians had was in terms of their culture and psyche they weren't necessarily militarily focused in terms of their attitudes and therefore local commanders held a significant amount of power in their respective brigades, autonomous to do what they wanted within those area, would then conform a general principle as dictated by a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you comment on your experience on whether -- the state of communications and the size of the territory for which the 3rd Corps was responsible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the whole of Bosnia communications were poor, not only were road lines of communication broken because of the front lines, the traditional means of military communications were now in different hands. Therefore, for secure communications they relied entirely on land line; i.e., you know, a line physically on the ground itself. They were often broken, therefore words of command were either normally given in person, in formal orders groups, or by individuals going on the ground, but quite often also on radio, and there were very little secure radio communications available at that time, therefore there was a great deal of intercepts between one side and another. So maintaining communication, maintaining command and control was therefore always going to be difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Speaking of command and control, from your own observations in 1993, can you comment on command and control within the 3rd Corps, starting with the commander and going down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think generally speaking it was a very difficult situation to be in. We ourselves weren't fully aware of what was going on on the ground. At the same time I doubt that they were fully aware of what was going on on the ground itself. I personally believe that General Enver Hadzihasanovic ran an efficient headquarters, but again, he was probably limited in terms of the quality of his officers further down the chain of command and at any one point if that chain was broken, then he would have serious problems. However we felt that, you know, he would give orders that would be either carried out or not carried out and depending on the individual receiving the order would depend entirely what action they took. Also we found, because of the nature of the Bosnian army, Bosnian Muslim army at that time, it was very localised in terms of attitudes and therefore individuals would carry out actions if it suited themselves to basically defend the position or attack a position to basically consolidate their lines. So, you know, no one was quite aware of actually what was going on all the time and that was one of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you referred a little earlier to a situation near Kacuni. Was that, based on your experience, an isolated incident or did this happen often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a classic example of a situation we always found ourselves in. Orders were given and either disobeyed because, not out of disrespect to the commanders but it didn't suit their needs at that time and therefore in many cases an order simply wasn't delivered. It may have been issued from the headquarters but because of the poor lines of communications at times they were either ignored or not delivered, so the incident at Kacuni was one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, talking about the commander, did he commit when required to do so, and when he did commit did you see the follow-up action on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as we were concerned, if ever we had a problem we'd go straight to the general, or Merdan or one of the subordinates would raise the issue. He would either get on a telephone or the radio or give us an officer to accompany us to the situation to resolve the matter, so they really bent over backwards. The same must be said also for the Croatians when they had the opportunity. So the commanders would do their best.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there please be pauses. The interpreters are finding it difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you please answer for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And could you provide the Trial Chamber with a definition of the term "Mujahedin" from your own experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been discussed a great deal, I'm sure. The situation in Yugoslavia at the time it was like a magnet to many individuals who were either giving military or humanitarian support. In our area of responsibility we never came across Mujahedin in any formal sense. We heard that elements from Islamic countries, also from Turkey, were coming into Bosnia. We didn't know physically where they were or under whose command and control they actually were. My interpretation of what Mujahedin is, it's a fighter of Islamic faith who sees himself fighting a Holy War, a Jihad in support of Islam. We knew that people were supporting the Bosnian government from the East but we weren't aware of their activities in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, do you believe, based on your experience, that the Mujahedin actually existed in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It would assist everybody in the courtroom if a pause was made between a question and an answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. We physically saw no evidence, as a battalion, of Mujahedin in any formal sense operating in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please slow down. The interpreters do not -- are not able to follow you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We shall try and do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, we had no physical evidence and we didn't physically see any Mujahedin operating in our area of responsibility. We heard that there were elements there. Certainly one of the commanders in 3 Corps in the Novi Seher area himself was complaining about elements further to his north in the Maglaj area and that they were essentially making that area more Islamic and causing problems but they weren't within, you know, his chain of command and could do nothing about them. We never -- I personally and I don't recall any of the members of BritBat seeing any foreign fighters from Middle Eastern countries within the ranks of the Bosnian army, but we did see a number of former British soldiers, Germans and the like there, but we always heard of reports of extremist activity or Mujahedin, we physically didn't have anything in our area that affected our operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a considerable delay in the French interpretation. You are too fast. The witness is too fast. The interpreters simply cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sir, do you want me to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, we will have to definitely slow down. My next question to you is, in your view, based on your own experience, did the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina exercise command and control over those Mujahedin that were in Central Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no evidence that they were within the order of battle of 3rd Corps. As I mentioned, we physically saw no physical Mujahedin presence in the area. The only time we heard of their activities was from the HVO or, in that one particular case in the Maglaj area, from one of General Hadzihasanovic's subordinates. But again, you know, we had no physical evidence that they were part of 3rd Corps, and whenever we challenged commanders about their activities, they said they were not within their -- they were not within their control. It was simple as that.
