utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Witness, was the issue of Mujahedin discussed at the Orders Group held by Colonel Stewart within BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- we'd hold a daily -- well, not Orders Group. It was a briefing at 5.00 every day where the day's activities were summarised by the liaison officer on the ground and also milinfosums were read out in terms of what was going on on the ground, and I don't recall Mujahedin activity ever featuring in any of the meetings I took place in. There simply wasn't an issue in our area. I think the term "Mujahedin" was used quite loosely. Whenever you spoke to the Bosnians -- or the Croats would often refer to the Serbs as "Chetniks," the Croats would be referred to as "Ustasha," and anybody who was seen to be, let's say devote in respect to Islam was referred to as "Mujahedin," but normally they were referred to in other derogatory terms. So I'm not sure whether, you know, it was a loose term, but that was what people were using and therefore it can get quite confusing in terms of what was actually going on on the ground, but as I mentioned, we had no physical evidence of who they were, who they were under the command and control of, or physically where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, was the Mujahedin a major issue or an issue when you were in Central Bosnia in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall it being an issue. I never recall any incident where Colonel Bob Stewart would go to General Hadzihasanovic or to Merdan to complain about the activities of the Mujahedin. In the same way, later in 1994, when working for General Rose, the only foreign fighters we had any dealings with in terms of the political aspect was with the Serbs, i.e., foreign fighters within their ranks in and around Sarajevo. So from a Bosnian Muslim perspective I can honestly say that we had no dealings with any aspect to do with Mujahedin. Maybe later on it became an issue but certainly while we were there it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Witness HC, when you attended meetings with Blaskic, did he ever complain about Mujahedin in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would normally complain about extremist activity, but I -- the term "Mujahedin" was never really mentioned if at all. But again, we couldn't independently verify any of these activities. You have to appreciate that our role wasn't there to gather intelligence or information about what the warring factions were doing. Our role was to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and that all our information gathering activity was to have that situational awareness, the picture of what was going on on the ground, and because their activities weren't influencing anything in terms of our area of responsibility, we had very little information on them and whoever we spoke to couldn't tell us the realities of what was happening on the ground with regard to their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, can you comment on the reliability of complaints made by Blaskic and by the HVO in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every side would open every meeting with a whole series of complaints. It was the accepted form. And again, you know, nine times out of ten we would verify that the complaints were actually untruths or were overexaggerated, and so whenever we went to meetings we'd always try independently to verify any complaints and if there were obviously falsehoods, we would then tell them, so you had to take everything with a pinch of salt, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, Witness HC, pertains to our knowledge of intelligence. Do you hold any qualifications in the intelligence world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of my work in two tours in Bosnia, and then after the war, once peace came into that region, I was identified to take over the role as the brigade and then divisional intelligence officer for the 1st Mechanised Brigade and then the multinational division south-west, based in Banja Luka. Prior to that appointment, I went on a divisional brigade level intelligence course to prepare me for the appointment and then spent 18 months prior to deployment with an intelligence organisation preparing the unit for the deployment. So that was my training and background. And then in 1999, between March and September, I was the divisional intelligence officer, Chief G2, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In 1999, when you were the chief intelligence officer for the multinational division south-west in Banja Luka, how did you gather intelligence? What resources did you have for this purpose, and were you successful in obtaining meaningful intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation in 1999 was very different to the situation we faced in Bosnia during the war. We were now operating within a NATO chain of command. We were therefore there in essentially a war fighting capacity, although at peace, and therefore we had at our beck and call all the national intelligence resources and well as NATO resources at hand. Although I'm an infantry officer with an intelligence background now, working to me I had a team of 14 intelligence operatives who were analysts, trained analysts. Each of those had responsibility looking at military, political, criminal, and other activities in our divisional area. We also had a whole series of liaison officers on the ground, both overt and covert. We relied heavily on human intelligence. We relied heavily on radio and telephone intercepts, and basically we were resourced for the task. At that time, the threats of airstrikes against Serbia as a result of what was going on in Kosovo was paramount and therefore our role was to identify what the Bosnian Serb army was going to do in the event of airstrikes to preempt any of their actions and also to identify what the forces of the federation were going to do in the event of the Serbs moving first, and therefore it was fundamental that the intelligence push, as it's been referred to, was there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would appreciate a pause, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, could you compare the intelligence gathered in 1999 when you were the chief intelligence officer with the information gathered in 1993 and found in the document called Milinfosum, if you know this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Milinfosums were military information summaries. They were essentially a summary of what liaison officers had found on the ground through their daily work in terms of what they felt was going on and from reports received from the various warring factions or political leaders. The difference is that in 1999, not only were we resourced to gather real intelligence but essentially speaking we could call on other information that could corroborate information from one source and another and therefore it was a true intelligence effort, whereas in the early days it was literally find out what was going on and report it and not necessarily always going to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So how would you -- how would you assess the reliability of the documents produced in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The documents produced at that time provided an overview of what the feeling was on the ground, provided an overview of what we were being informed by the various commanders on the ground or the situation that the troops found themselves in, but the problem was that we were very reliant on individuals within the entities providing that information, and in many cases, you know, what they found out was put on there. Everything was then sent further up the chain of command where we assumed they would then be corroborated with other information but nothing ever came back down to us in terms of direction or strategic intelligence at that time. So it was just simply a one-way flow of information, not intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, a quick question, Witness HC: Gathering intelligence, in your professional opinion, is that something that requires qualifications and resources or can anybody do that, to gather meaningful intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anyone can gather -- anyone can gather information but then how that information is then used and turned into intelligence is an art in many respects. That's why we had trained intelligence operatives working in divisional headquarters for that task. Within battle groups, intelligence staff are simply individuals plucked from the ranks and they are not resourced in the same way as a modern army would be in terms of a divisional level. It's just basically information gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why did this system change in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the system really changed in 1996 when NATO took over in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Up until then, we were not -- the UN up to 1995, 1996, was viewed as an impartial element. We had no real power or influence on any of the warring factions, but of course when the mandate changed and it became a NATO operation, all the sides had to be compliant to the rules and regulations laid down by the Dayton Accord, and of course we were now part of the problem in Bosnia. Of course we had complete control over the activities of the entities, we had complete freedom of movement and we were able to bring additional assets to fulfil the mission. So the whole operational situation had changed completely. The two can't be compared in that respect as being alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, I have one last question for you, and that is can you confirm that in your second tour in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you mentioned you were there in 1994, who you had dealings with in terms of the high level representatives of the warring factions. And I'm talking of personal access and dealings with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the personal aid and interpreter to General Sir Michael Rose and so I acted on his behalf, either independently or in his presence, with all the main political and military leaders of Bosnian Serb army, the Bosnian Croats, and the Bosnian Muslims part of the federation, so from a Serb side, personal access to General Mladic, General Gvero, General Milovanovic, as well as their subordinates. On the political level, all the meetings attended by General Rose and the UN with Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, Plavsic; on the Bosnian Muslim side, access to President Izetbegovic, General Delic on occasions when we deployed on the ground around Visoko, with General Hadzihasanovic who was at that time chief of staff, as well as corps commanders and brigade commanders; and then on the Croatian side again returning to General Petkovic and Prlic who was the -- who was the political aspect. So full access to all these individuals. And I was the interpreter at all these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, Witness HC, that was my before last question. My last question is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to notify everybody in the courtroom that there is a significant delay in the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in your dealings with all these top level personalities from all the warring factions, whether the Mujahedin issue, whether it was an issue and whether it was discussed as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was never discussed. The only elements of foreign fighters that caused concern were those on the Serb side in Sarajevo who again, according to the Serbs, were out of their control and actually they were then eliminated but what we feel were elements from within Serbia itself brought in to destroy that element in around the Jewish cemetery. So to the best of my knowledge and recollection, the issue of Mujahedin was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness HC, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting because there was four minutes' delay between what the witness was saying and the interpretation. I think in the B/C/S booth it must have been a similar situation. And the interpretation hasn't ended yet. The other Defence team, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We do have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Witness HC, is it correct that you left Central Bosnia in early May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I left on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You've mentioned a number of personalities that you met. It is correct, is it not, that when you were on the ground, up until early May 1993, you never met anyone from the command of the 7th Brigade of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't meet anyone from the 7th Brigade, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And it's also correct that you had no reason to seek a meeting with the command of the 7th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. We heard of their activities in certain areas, but we had no -- I physically had no dealings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In fact, you had very limited information about their composition, their operations, and their activities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: This was the same for many of the brigades within the 3rd Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: If you were, therefore, shown any documents from the 7th Brigade, either internal documents or documents between the brigade and its command in the 3rd Corps, you would not be able to comment on the accuracy of any of the information contained in those documents or any of the matters referred to; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unless I was involved with any of the incidents referred within the documents, then I couldn't be able to comment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You said in your evidence-in-chief that you never saw any of these Mujahedin elements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Would it therefore be right that you have no evidence that any of these different Mujahedin elements were ever effectively controlled by the 3rd Corps Command or any of the brigades within the 3rd Corps including the 7th Brigade? Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct. The only time we heard about them being physically active was in the area around Maglaj, and that came from Colonel Jozic, who was the commander there, and he stated they were not part of his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You never had any opportunity to meet that particular group of Mujahedin in that area, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We had no reason to go and see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness HC. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now looking at the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness HC, my name is Matthias Neuner, and along with my colleagues I am appearing here on behalf of the Prosecution, and I am going to put a couple of questions to you. First of all, let me start off with your 18-month intelligence training. Can you tell the Trial Chamber again, in what year did you engage in that intelligence training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started the appointment in 1997, and I actually deployed in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So my question is, before you came to Central Bosnia, did you also have any training in intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the dates of your stay in the Central Bosnia area, I have written down here that you came to the Central Bosnian area in November 1992 and left at some point in February 1993 for Eastern Bosnia. Can you please clarify the dates, from when to when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- of your first stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically having deployed in November of 1992, most of activities were in Central Bosnia. Around the 7th of December of 1992, that's when we started moving to the eastern area, particularly around Tuzla because of the situation there, and essentially on a weekly basis between January 1993 and April of 1993 I would spend either all of my time in Vitez or all of my time in Tuzla on an exchange between two offices. On certain occasions we would be in Tuzla for two or three days and then go back to Central Bosnia. So in terms of the overall operational picture, at times we were away from the activities in Central Bosnia and so we were literally flitting from one area to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. So -- but can you tell the Trial Chamber the majority of your time you either spent in Eastern Bosnia or in Central Bosnia, meaning the Vitez area --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably half and half. There were two of us and we would literally do time in Vitez and time in Tuzla on exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you testified already on 6 May you left the area. I'm referring to 1993. And you returned in January 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To stay until what time in Bosnia, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact date I can't recall, but it was the beginning of July. So literally either -- either -- I left probably Sarajevo in the last week of June and then returned back to the UK first week of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And during that stay in 1994, did you also go to Vitez area frequently or did you, rather, stay in other areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very infrequently. The only time we went to Vitez was when we established the federation as a result of the negotiations that took place in around March of 1994. That was then the occasion. I then met General Blaskic, as he was then, and so we probably visited Vitez, in that six months, probably four or five times. Most of our activity was directed in around Sarajevo and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand you said you visited Vitez four or time times. For long stays or just for temporary stays, like for one meeting and then you returned to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very short meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Very short meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may ask, from November 1992 towards 6th of May, 1993, you stayed in Central Bosnia for a longer time, not only for short meetings. Where were you stationed, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in the Nova Bila base within Vitez. Obviously living in houses there within the old school building area, and then whenever we were in Tuzla we were in the air base in Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So on a weekly basis from November 1992 to May 1993, how many days on average would you spend in Nova Bila base? Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From -- from December through to January I'd probably spent five days in Nova Bila and then probably two days in Tuzla. When the situation around Srebrenica became tense and at Cerska in around February-March time I spent probably a solid month in Tuzla around March, working from Tuzla to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to ask a little bit about your tasks. You said already you translated. How many international translators were with you employed at the time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean international? From --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As opposed to local translators coming from the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you were the only international translator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was two of us, both of us were British army officers. The third was compromised in Croatia right at the beginning of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And this first person or international translator, do you know his name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was compromised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Not the one in Croatia but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let us go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness HC, I was just asking, you have met Mr. Blaskic. You have met Mr. Kordic and other high-ranking personalities from the ABiH and from the HVO, and this was in the capacity of translating for your colleagues, meaning the colleagues on behalf -- the colleagues of ECMM or mostly probably BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly BritBat but again I say nine times of out of ten I wouldn't necessarily translate, I would listen to what was being said because they preferred to use their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And within BritBat you stated for a certain point in time you were the only translator. Did you then perform these translations or did local colleagues perform these translations? Please just clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only times I did physically the translations themselves if a local colleague wasn't available or a local colleague couldn't go to a meeting because the other side doesn't allow the other faith to be there or the other party. So in peaceful situations the locals do the interpreting. I would be there present within the meeting to listen in and provide advice and inform our commanders what else was being said apart from that being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So in your capacity attending the meetings as interpreter or not, would you -- would you appear as part of the delegation when you were going there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The normal form was that the delegation would be the principal officers attending. Whenever we went to a meeting we'd have our interpreters and also liaison officers and nine times out of ten we wouldn't be part of the official delegation and therefore minuted on the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand from your answer that probably - and this is actually a question - you were appearing on the meeting minutes as part of the delegation, or probably not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So only the high-level people would be mentioned while you in person wouldn't be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Neither as interpreter nor as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was never the form. You'd only really state on the form who was present in terms of the actual parties themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart has testified here. You heard already from my learned friend. And he has testified about 5.00 p.m. meetings within BritBat. Can you report for the purpose of these 5.00 p.m. meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can probably imagine, throughout the day we had officers deployed in the countryside gathering information, obviously on patrol trying to resolve any situations. So every day at 5.00 the commanding officer would have his O Group, his Orders Group, where everyone came back, everyone would report on their activities and information would be passed. The intent for the next day would be given and we would then break up. So it was the opportunity for the command to be made fully aware of what was happening on the ground as far as they were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So is it a fair summary it was a kind of brainstorm meeting about the information gathered, and you said later on information was passed on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically the meeting would take the form of -- a situation report would be given by the battalion intelligence officer in terms of the reports that had been presented to him from the liaison officers. Once that had been completed, the operations officer would then inform everybody what task had been completed that day and what the next tasks were for the following day. At the end the commanding officer would say a few words in terms of his summary on what was going on on the ground and provide his own intent for the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who would write reports, the so-called Cheshire milinfosums? Who would write these reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every single patrol that went on the ground had to come back and the formal report had to be written by the patrol commander in terms of what information they had gathered. That information would then be given to the intelligence officer who was a member of the battalion who would then consolidate that information in the Milinfosum report itself; on the operations side, the Operations Officer would then write the current operations paragraph of the daily situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I take it from your answer an intelligence and an operations officer within BritBat were involved in producing the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The intelligence officer was responsible for producing the milinfosum. The operations officer was responsible for producing the situation report. There were two distinct reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. And what was the education of that intelligence officer usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was just a battalion officer who had been selected by the commanding officer to be the IO, the intelligence officer for the battalion. He may have attended a six-week course but had no -- he didn't have -- he didn't have intelligence staff working to him; it was simply his own staff and within the battalion. So it was very low-level intelligence as opposed to strategic intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You're referring to a six-week course. Was this course in the former Yugoslavia? Was this course in Britain? Was this course somewhere else? What was the content of such a course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a six-week battalion and brigade level intelligence officers course. It's really looking at how intelligence is gathered, and the majority of the course is directed towards what was formally Soviet doctrine in terms of -- so from a war fighting perspective, how to fight the intelligence war in modern western armies. Prior to any deployment to the former Yugoslavia, the intelligence officer would receive essentially information summaries from the high headquarters keeping him abreast of what was going on so he could prepare himself and his staff for the deployment, but there was no specific intelligence gathering training for intelligence officers deploying to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. And you just said before the intelligence officer would be used in -- for a particular task in terms of putting these milinfosums together. He would already read, digest, so to speak, analyse previous reports, probably milinfosums or other information? What type of information would he have access to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a key to all his work. The key thing is to gather the information, look at it, compare it with other information, look at where the information came from, who was the source and make an assessment on the information. If you produce a report without an assessment or a comment, it's useless. And therefore the key to any work of that nature is to be aware of all of the facts and corroborate it. In terms of resources, all he had was what the patrols were seeing and hearing on the ground and bringing back to him. So that was the limitation of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We're just talking about the important part being the assessment. In the milinfosums would that be the comment field, meaning first there is a kind of factual description probably of what the intelligence officer had learned and then there is a comment field? Would that relate to the analysis, the analysis of the intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the key part. The first part, the information, is just information. The comment is, therefore, the intelligence officer's summary of that information in context with everything else. Quite often there wasn't a comment, and therefore a few days later, once more information was gathered, a comment would then be made because all the facts were then available. So it was the comment aspect that was critical to provide commanders the assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I can just - with the assistance of the usher - show an exhibit to you. And this is actually a document from 27 of January. So we have enough copies for everybody available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt at this point but we might be back to the earlier discussion we had this morning. This, I suspect, is the new document that may be marked for identification, but in our submission it can only be shown to the witness if it is going to be used to seek to refresh his memory or challenge his credibility. The way I understand the evidence being given now is for the purposes of obtaining information about how military information summaries were prepared, and I don't see how this can be shown to the witness under Your Honour's ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm prepared to ask some -- to lay a foundation to ask some more questions and then try to pursue the matter further or drop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness HC, we were just talking about the reports, milinfosums, and do you have any recollection from the time you have been on the ground in Central Bosnia that these milinfosums contained also information on Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was ever mentioned by any of the field officers who was on the ground, it would be mentioned within the actual milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the basis for such a Milinfosum was a prior mentioning. Would this prior mentioning usually be done in the 5.00 p.m. meeting at the BritBat headquarter or was it some -- could that mentioning be, let's say, in every daily life or the daily tasks of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If anything was mentioned in the course of an officer's normal activity out on the ground - for example, the liaison officer who was working in the Novi Seher area would receive from the commander the presence of, let's say, Mujahedin or extremists in the area - then that information would be given at that end of that patrol to the intelligence officer who would then include it as a comment within the intelligence summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes. In late January there was a Milinfosum information report about the Travnik area and this mentioned also the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in one of its sections. Do you recall any Milinfosum being written about foreigners or Mujahedin in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade? Do you remember this being ever subject of a Milinfosum from your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without reading the Milinfosum I can't recall. The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was always, in many respects, highlighted by the fact that it always had that label "Muslimanski" in that respect. And so people automatically assumed that it was more Islamic than the rest of the elements within 3 Corps or the Bosnian army. We knew that in the Travnik area that there were foreign fighters from Britain, from other nations, apparently from the Middle East. But again, I don't recall any of our officers reporting seeing any formed Mujahedin elements in that area. But whether it was confused with the Muslimanski Brigade, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would it help you if I show you a report? Would that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, can I please have the document distributed. It's in the binder you find then in front of you. It's actually tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, it is quite clear that the Prosecution is endeavouring once again to use the decision of the Chamber for purposes that were not envisaged by that decision. When the Chamber rendered its decision that the document can be used to refresh the memory of the witness, that is in the case that the witness does not remember an event and then he is reminded of that event. If you ask a witness, "Have you seen a report on such-and-such an event" so much later, this is a way of bypassing the gist of the decision. The Prosecution could have easily tendered this document as a Prosecution Exhibit, and I think that because this is being done we are wasting a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the Prosecution going to tell us? Since the document you wish to show is the dated the 27th of January, it is Milinfosum 88. So the first question that should have been put to the witness is whether the witness was present at that meeting of the 27th of January. Then if he said yes, we could refresh his memory. If not, you are going along the lines suggested by the Defence. You are showing him a document to make him discuss an event which was not the subject of the examination-in-chief or which is not linked to questions put by the Defence. Can the Prosecution clarify us as to the purpose of showing him this document, which is in English tab 3, in view of the objection made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. When asked by my learned friend Mr. Dixon, this witness has said he had very little information on the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade available at the time. On the 27th of January, the witness has also testified that he was in the area attending a meeting. So I discussed with him at 5.00 p.m. -- at the 5.00 p.m. meetings basically issues relating to milinfosums were also discussed, and I asked him whether he was familiar with any reports being written in milinfosums about the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and the witness himself asked me to show him a report and refresh his memory. I was actually not pushing that point further, I was even asked by the witness to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, on the 27th of January, were you present at this 5.00 meeting which preceded the drafting of Milinfosum 88, to the best of your recollection? Were you there or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in Vitez at the time, I would have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do not exclude the possibility of being present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the Prosecution, you may try to refresh the memory of the witness on the understanding that he may have been present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness HC, if you please look at tab number 3 and you see the Milinfosum is number 88 from 27 January. Just look at the third passage, is mentioned in the header Travnik, and there please just read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "A normally reliable source -" and it's got 1 Cheshire, 27 of January 1993 - "has provided additional information on the 7th Muslimanski Brigade. He confirmed that this brigade is commanded from Zenica with battalions deployed within 3 Corps area. A battalion from 7 Brigade is deployed on the front line in the Travnik area. Members of the battalion consider themselves Mujahedin in every sense. The majority of members are staunch practising Muslims recruited from the local area. Although this particular battalion was instructed by two Iranians the source commented that external Mujahedin from Islamic countries within the brigade numbered at the most 100 to 150. A number of 7 Brigade soldiers on checkpoints north of Vitez were noted wearing a cap badge consisting of a green Muslim crescent, insert --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read more slowly. Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. "A number of 7 Brigade soldiers on checkpoints north of Vitez were noted wearing a cap badge consisting of a green Muslim crescent insert with a gold star. They stated that this was the insignia for the Muslimanski Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Having just read this out, does this refresh your recollection in any event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms that at these meetings whenever someone mentioned the presence of the extremist Mujahedin it would have been mentioned -- it would have been included in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You testified earlier about the knowledge within BritBat about, yes, Mujahedin being involved or being not involved with the ABiH. Does this show to you that there was indeed information available at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is just one report. It's not come from one of our soldiers on the grounds that if I quote "a normally reliable source," that would have been an external element. And again, from an intelligence perspective, there is no comment. So this report in itself doesn't prove anything, with great respect. A normally reliable source is somebody who will provide information routinely that will prove to be accurate. That's not to say that occasionally the information wasn't accurate. What would now normally happen is that this information would be held, if possible investigated, and then subsequently a comment would be given in terms of the truth of the actual report itself. Again, from experience, it's quite difficult to take everything as a truth. One of the issues that was always exaggerated in Bosnia by all sides was numbers. To say, you know, a hundred, 250 soldiers from Islamic countries, you know -- I'll give you one example: We were told once that there were 1.500 wounded in one particular area and we only found 75. So numbers can be exaggerated. But this in itself is just one piece of information that's part of a jigsaw and it would have been briefed but it in no way to me confirms the presence of Mujahedin in the area because, as I mentioned, we physically didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is half past twelve. We will have our customary break and resume work about five to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, again. Witness HC, you testified today on page 66, line 22, that in relation to the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, you heard about their activities in certain areas. Can you elaborate a little bit what you mean by certain areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I can't see anything on the screen. Should I be able to see something on the screen here? Thank you. We knew that the brigade was based in around Zenica. I don't recall any of our call-signs on the ground ever coming across them or seeing them actually operating in the area, but what was always drawn to our attention was the fact that their title had the "Muslimanski" aspect to it and that was always therefore -- seemed to be different to the rest of the 3rd Corps units. But personally I never came across any members of the Muslimanski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You say seems to be different in relation to other 3rd Corps units, what do you mean by different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the perception was that the majority of the soldiers within the 3rd Corps and the Bosnian army were just normal people who happened to be Muslims. This brigade looks like to be a manoeuvre element who were drawn from let us imagine all of Bosnia who had, you know, particular beliefs stronger than the rest of the army, and they were therefore titled Muslimanski Brigade. Because of that title, it drew our attention. But as I said, you know, they weren't physically operating or operating when we were physically there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just testified about -- that this brigade was a kind of manoeuvre element. Can you elaborate what you mean by manoeuvre element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had very little information on the brigade as I've already mentioned. But, you know, by the nature of its organisation -- the majority of the brigades were geographically based. To that extent, many soldiers were reluctant to move from one area to actually act somewhere else because by doing so they would relieve, you know, -- well, they would essentially vacate the area they were responsible for and therefore, in many respects, would be vulnerable to attack. From the information I recall at that time, because the Muslimanski Brigade wasn't necessarily geographically located defending a particular area of the line, it had the ability to move to different areas if it was required as a -- I can't imagine if it was an all-arms formation, but certainly it was not geographically static like the vast majority of the Bosnian army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember what its commander, the name of the commander when you arrived in Central Bosnia in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never met the commander, so no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want now to switch to what you said on page 60 of the transcript, around line 23 about complaints during negotiations or meetings. And you said every side complained to us or to the audience at these meetings, and nine out of ten claims which were made on these meetings proved to be unfounded. Does this apply to both complaints of the HVO and of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, we'd go to a meeting and the first thing that would happen is that every side would explain what the other side had been doing in violation of any agreements, and of course the majority of times this information was passed up from its units on the grounds and then articulated to us. But we had no opportunity to independently verify what was going on, and whenever we did verify what was going on we often found that the complaints were unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So and you're referring with complaints -- complaints of ABiH and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn to what you said on page 54, around line 20. You talked about secure communications of the ABiH and that they relied entirely on land lines. With land lines you're referring to telephone lines which are physically in the ground, I assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is it. I mean, it's difficult to communicate at the best of times, and therefore both sides were predominantly using insecure radio communications for routine information at a local level, but they knew that could be intercepted quite easily by the opposing forces. Therefore, the only guaranteed means of communication was by using the telephone network. But again, if that telephone network crossed a front line, it could be tapped into. And so, you know, at the end of the day communications could not be relied on to be secure at all times. The same applied to us as well. They were listening to what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever visit the 3rd Corps communication centre while you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the information you got about the land lines, did you get this information from the ABiH itself or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We just knew from our own intelligence in terms of how the former Yugoslav army operated. Essentially, if you imagine, when the war started they would have carried on as they would have done had they still been in Yugoslavia. That's how the system of defence was organised. If you imagine historically, the Yugoslav army was there very much organised to defend its borders and its interior from external attack and therefore all infrastructure was in place for that purpose. What they never envisaged was the attack coming from within and therefore breaking down the normal communication that would have been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recall giving or providing information to the ICTY in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you wish, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Let me ask the President to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness HC, on 25th of January, 1993, you encountered -- you describe the encounter at the barricade in Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that you spoke to a couple of local soldiers there. Do you remember from which unit the soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What unit patches they were wearing? Do you recall any specifics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I mean, at some stage around that time in the Kacuni area I recall seeing while I was with Colonel Bob Stewart and the regimental sergeant-major two individuals, not necessarily at that time who were wearing green bandannas, but again they didn't have any insignia on them. At the time I wasn't aware whether they were part of the Muslimanski Brigade or what. But whoever was a local unit in that area, they were the soldiers from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you're referring to green bandannas. Green bandannas would be worn at the time by the ABiH, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not across the board. And these were just two individuals. They weren't of any eastern origin. They were local individuals who were wearing a sort of green headband.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Local individuals from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the barrier was there because otherwise it would -- the area would be essentially exposed to entry for the HVO into the Kacuni area. You testified to that extent on page 46. Do you recall that a place called Lasva, a place called Dusina wasn't that far from the Kacuni barrier at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the whole Lasva Valley essentially, and it was a single road that was going through from Busovaca to Kiseljak. So that's why the barrier was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So do you recall the distances? How far was it to go to Lasva from Kacuni -- from the Kacuni barrier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Top of my head, without looking at a map, I wouldn't be able to give an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I would show you a map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- would that help you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher. This can please be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the area of the Kacuni checkpoint in relation to the road going from the Vitez area down to Kiseljak. And essentially the main area of fighting that we were concerned with were all the pockets of resistance, be they Bosnian Croat or Bosnian Muslim, from Busovaca, down to Kacuni and beyond. And this was known as the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't know what documents -- document is being used by the witness and the line that he has indicated, we don't know what they are. Maybe my learned friend could provide us with some information. What is the line that is across the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Prosecution tell us something about the map? Is that a map that has already been admitted? Is it a new map? And the line across the map, what does it represent, the line that cuts the map in two halves? What is that line all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The whole map about the whole area has been tendered into evidence. My understanding - and I talked to the mapping unit about it - is that this line is a kind of support line which is in the ground. So it's below the surface. That's what the mapping unit explained to me. It has no other relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document P98. Could you, Mr. Registrar, give us document P98.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the standard map that we were using at the time. Not only did it show the geography and features on the ground but also telegraph lines, power cables and everything else. So you'll see in this area here the articulation of masts which were either radio communications masts or telegraph lines. So if I recall, they were probably either underground or over ground telegraph lines or power lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show this map to Mr. Bourgon. The Defence, are you satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As you -- can you please mark where the Kacuni checkpoint was on that map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kacuni checkpoint was in this region here and the Busovaca area is there. This is the main road going to Zenica from the Kiseljak area. Turning left takes you to Vitez where the British base was. Turning right takes you on towards Zenica further to the north. And as you've asked, Merdani is in the area here, and the Lasva area is there. But that was known as the Lasva Valley to ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you point to Dusina, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusina is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How far away from Kacuni is Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every one of these grid references is approximately a kilometre, so that's five or six kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So this checkpoint was -- not checkpoint. This barricade was established five kilometres away from Dusina; is that correct? As the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the crow flies, and in order to get there, clearly that was a lot further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to mark where the Kacuni barrier was on the 25th of January, 1993, and place -- and circle the location and place a 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, and it's not necessarily accurate as far as my memory goes, I imagine it was probably in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And can you now encircle, please, Dusina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And make a 2 next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on. I want to move on, go back to the issues of Mujahedin. You yourself said you didn't see physically any Mujahedin, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you said that basically members of your BritBat battalion didn't also encounter any Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall any encounters with Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I state to you that BritBat Commander Stewart, who has testified earlier, said that he had personally seen Mujahedin at roadblocks of the mountain road between Zenica and Dubrovac - this is on page 83 of the LiveNote transcript from Monday this week - do you recall that he ever mentioned having seen Mujahedin on the roadblock between Zenica and Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You also said that Mujahedin were never mentioned on any meetings which you attended between the parties, ABiH and HVO. Did you attend joint commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily joint commission meetings, no. The only meeting I held at that time, was present at, was the meeting in Kiseljak afterwards which the joint commission was established. They were solely the meetings organised by ECMM, the two sides and also what we referred to as United Kingdom liaison officers who were sent from the UK into the area specifically for that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Is this the meeting on 30th of January which was attended by Mr. Fleming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I wasn't present at that meeting, within the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Within the meeting itself you weren't present. And have you seen the minute meetings maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would it help you if I show the meeting minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is P922, Prosecution Exhibit P922, if I may ask the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is part of the Defence documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It should be tab 2, then, I assume. Actually, this is the Prosecution -- these are the Prosecution documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is a Prosecution document, but it seems that the Defence have provided us with that in their binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is something that I have discussed with the witness. He said that he was not at the meeting but he remembers the meeting. This is a document that he had not seen, that he was not at the meeting. So maybe the -- my learned friend should establish the foundation, legal foundation for this question and showing the witness this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document will probably serve to refresh the witness's memory, but can you use some introductory questions in order to introduce this document because the witness doesn't know it and he was not present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand you have not been present at the meeting but you testified earlier you saw a picture about the meeting and you were in the vicinity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there when they all arrived, because there was a huge media circus essentially because of the significance of the meeting, and once the meeting started they all moved inside the building and those of us who weren't privy to the meeting stayed outside, and again I've -- I've never seen these minutes prior to coming here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand you've never seen those minutes. And did you speak to anybody else after the meeting - for example, your colleagues - about what has been discussed on the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. I don't recall, to be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak directly into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In this instance I guess if I refer to mentioning made by Mr. Fleming that the Mujahedin had been in the hills, which is drawn from his -- from the minutes of this meeting here, this wouldn't say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The point is if they're in the hills, we weren't because we were limited to the lines of communication physically on the roads, which was again a weakness of our operation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it would be good to know whether this person knows Mr. Fleming, because he was not at the meeting. And if he had spoken with Mr. Fleming, does he know what position was Mr. Fleming at. We don't know anything. This document has been admitted into evidence but this witness is not well suited to talk about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's not familiar with the contents of the document, he doesn't know what Mr. Fleming said, and he doesn't know him. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were you ever at the joint Busovaca commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were never. So, therefore, you probably did also have no knowledge about the issue of Mujahedin discussed there. Maybe some of your colleagues went back from these meetings and mentioned something about the issue of Mujahedin being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the report says on page 3, "He requested restraint in spreading the rumours of increased tensions." There was a lot of talk at all these meetings about extremists and the like, but we couldn't physically confirm their presence. You know, I physically didn't see any Eastern soldiers operating within the area of responsibility, and as already mentioned, in Kacuni the only two individuals I saw who were wearing green bandannas were the Bosnians themselves. So they may have been, let's say, from 7th Muslimanski Brigade, I don't know because they had no unit insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I was just asking you for meetings which were going on at the time about the -- which also dealt with Mujahedin issues. What I actually tried to explore was the basis on which you said today that the Mujahedin were out of control of the ABiH at the time. Did you learn that information from the 3rd Corps itself or from which sources did you learn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ultimately the information came from our liaison officers. We could not establish any direct link between 3rd Corps and any of those elements operating within Bosnia itself in 3rd Corps area or elsewhere, and certainly when the liaison officer spoke to the commander of the Novi Seher area he was the individual who informed him of the presence of Islamic elements in the Maglaj area who were out of his control and could do nothing about them. So all our information came from the various warring factions themselves, which is why we had to rely on the sources because the information provided by the sources wasn't always going to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At the time, were you yourself tasked in getting information on the Mujahedin or were other colleagues tasked with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall a specific task. I certainly wasn't tasked to gather information on Mujahedin activities. I don't recall any specific direction being given to any of the liaison officers to gather intelligence. Anything they gained was purely through conversations or their own reports, because at that time there were many people operating in and around Bosnia. There were many aid convoys moving through and therefore it was difficult -- they weren't there, in my view, as a group on the side of the road advertising themselves as Mujahedin. It just didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So in other words, since you weren't tasked with this, others were tasked with this probably sensitive job, and in a way that's all you know, that others were tasked in gathering intelligence on Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe people were physically tasked to do it. In terms of their routine actions on the ground they may have found out information and then, as you saw with the Milinfosum, reported it "from a normally reliable source," but as I mentioned with that Milinfosum, there is no comments and therefore it will be interesting to see subsequent reports whether or not that was actually confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Since you weren't the commander of BritBat at the time, you did not necessarily need to know whether people were tasked within --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been mentioned at a 5.00 briefing for that particular tasking, but of course if I wasn't there for that 5.00 meeting and it was mentioned, I wouldn't know, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You testified briefly about Hadzihasanovic, about Merdan, about Blaskic and Kordic. You all met them at meetings. But my understanding is at these meetings basically you were accompanying other high level members of BritBat. So your own capacity in which you appeared on this meeting was not an exposed capacity but was more or less an assisting capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I had no formal directed role to play in these meetings which is why I never appeared on any of the minutes of the meeting as taking part. I was there because I was in the area and it was always useful to have one of your own officers who speaks the language to be able to verify what's been said, and with all the best in the world, interpreters do make mistakes, and it's those mistakes that can be critical in any meeting and I was there to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- reinforce in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So in other words, from November 1992 throughout May 1993, you didn't perform any superior role within BritBat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not within the BritBat area, but I did in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In Eastern Bosnia. I leave it here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: No further questions on behalf of the Prosecution at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Defence have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, I have a few short questions for you, the first one being: Did your intelligence training in 1997 help you to understand the value of the gathering of information and the production of milinfo summaries in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were obviously trained to do things properly in terms of intelligence assessments. There is a difference between intelligence assessment and a Milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe, Witness HC, the procedure that you would follow, you and your staff in 1999, when obtaining a piece of information from someone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information would be received. It was read by an analyst operating on that particular speciality. He would then add a comment. That would then be cross-referenced against an intelligence database that would be maintained on individuals' activities to see if there is any linkages towards that information. Once that information was therefore corroborated with evidence that we already had, or if it wasn't, we would then issue an intelligence tasking to a call-sign on the ground, a unit who would go onto the ground to confirm or deny the reports. Occasionally that wasn't possible so that would then be stored and then if subsequent information was released, it would then be cross-referenced and again an intelligence assessment would be made on that. We never used a single piece of evidence as an example of fact on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you obtain some information as to the origin of the information or on the source of the source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each piece of evidence had to be referenced in terms of who provided it and the source would be graded in accordance with their reliability. So for example, a perfect source would be an A1 source and therefore you would then grade it A, B, C and so on and so forth. We wouldn't grade, from an intelligence perspective, a normally reliable source, it would be a physical A1 to E5 grading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Witness HC, what is the value, in your opinion, of single source information obtained if it is not verified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be dangerous. Therefore it shouldn't be used in isolation but however it does, as previously mentioned, add to the jigsaw of the picture, but the important thing is that every piece of information has to be corroborated with more than one source to be of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned in response to a question from my colleague that there were lots of rumours in 1993. In your opinion, can a rumour unfortunately become an erroneous fact simply because it is repeated many times in documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think people will start --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Objection. This was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the re-examination, the party asking questions is not allowed to ask leading questions, because we are not in the cross-examination stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is a question about the opinion of the witness. Does erroneous information which appears several times in documents could unfortunately become a fact even though it is erroneous. This is a question. It is not a leading question. It is simply asking the witness for his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Why in your opinion is the question a leading one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It suggests the answer as the question as such was put, and in addition, this is a fact witness, Your Honour, and inasmuch an opinion. The Prosecution is of the opinion that it is not the right moment to ask from a fact witness an opinion about how things are or how things are not. This is certainly an issue which is left to Your Honours to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, the Prosecution tells us that this is a fact witness, and in fact indeed he was an interpreter who was present on the ground and that you're asking him a question that goes facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect for the opinion of my learned friend, he has asked several questions about the process of collecting information in the cross-examination, and my question has to do with this process, and the witness is able to give a general opinion, not as an expert. But I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Go ahead, as the Chamber can authorise you to put such a question, we are doing that. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The last issue concerning an information appearing in many documents can it unfortunately become a fact even though it is erroneous? Is this something you are familiar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's could quite easily be a fact. But that's the job, therefore, of the trained intelligence analyst to look at the facts as they are and provide an assessment on the reality. The problem was in a battalion they would not necessarily have the training to make that assessment, and with so much such information, or let's say misinformation flowing around the command, it's quite easy for these facts to be sort of misconstrued as the truth or not the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, you mention in response to a question from my colleague that there was a difference between mil information summary and daily information report. Can you bring a little more information on this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you refer to a daily situation report as opposed to information report. The reason why they were called milinfosums was because we were not in a war fighting capacity, we were not there to gather intelligence, and therefore we couldn't present intelligence reports in that sort of operation. They were therefore called information summaries. They basically provided feedback to the chain of command on what was going on on the ground in accordance with entities involved with the fighting. The situation report would have a very short summary of the intelligence or information picture and then concentrate more on our own activities in terms of what we were doing today and what will be happening tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, in response to a question from my colleague, you mentioned that both sides would sometimes complain and that when the complaint was verified, it was shown to be unfounded. My question to you is did this happen more often with one side than the other, and if so, what side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it's a generalisation, but quite often the majority of the complaints came from the HVO side about activities of the ABiH and again most of the time they were found to be unfounded. I recall a particular incident in Kula, which again is on this map, whereby we were asked to investigate activities by the Bosnian army against the Croat positions in Kula in breach of the cease-fire. When we arrived on the position, there was no fighting going on. We then moved on to the Bosnian position, and while we were actually on there we were attacked by the Croats. So that was one example where they used Bosnian activity to force us into an area and while we were in that area we were then attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness HC, you were asked whether when you attended meetings with high officials such as Hadzihasanovic and Merdan whether you were accompanied by some persons. My question is very simple: Did you -- did the persons who were leading those meetings, the high-level officers that you were accompanying, in your view, did they share your assessment of General Hadzihasanovic and Merdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two more questions and I'm done. You were mention something about the federation being set up and attending a meeting in Vitez in March 1994. My question to you is: Was the Mujahedin an issue of contention between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats when establishing the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. The only time I then recall subsequently as part of the Dayton Accord was withdrawal of any foreign forces from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But in terms of the establishment of the federation itself, again that wasn't part of any of the negotiations that was taking place at that time chaired by Brigadier Wreath who was the commander of MND south-west at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness HC. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. The Prosecution wishes to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution just wishes to state that the last two issues didn't arise directly out of the cross-examination of the Prosecution, meaning the two meetings including the negotiations about the establishment of the federation. At no point in time did the Prosecution ask any questions in relation to this, and we just want to have this stated for the record. And in addition, there was also a withdrawal mentioned. This is page 107, line 13. After the Dayton Accord about the withdrawal of any foreigners. These are completely new issues which haven't been touched upon at all by the Prosecution during its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, the Prosecution is telling us that these two issues, according to them, do not emanate from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the opinion of the Defence, those questions did emanate from the intention of the Prosecution to show that the witness did not have occasion to hear discussions of the Mujahedin. The Defence is showing that if there was one place where he could have heard about the Mujahedin it was then, and he was present then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber takes note. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Only a few questions arising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that two minutes, three minutes, because we're overstepping our time already.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in your testimony that there was something of a difference between the 7th Brigade and you mentioned that had it was a manoeuvre brigade. To some extent we are again covering old ground that was dealt with in the Prosecution case. You won't know this, but there have been international witnesses including, you might know this person, Mark Bower, who have confirmed that there were various manoeuvre brigades within the 3rd Corps.
